description: An introduction to static electricity, covering how objects become charged by friction and induction, the law of charges, conductors and insulators, and everyday applications such as capacitors and lightning conductors.

mcq.questionText: Static electricity is best described as:

options.text: Electricity that flows continuously in a wire
An electric charge that stays at rest on an object

mcq.explanation: Static electricity is charge that builds up and stays on an object. Exam Tip: Static (charge at rest) differs from current electricity (charge flowing).

mcq.questionText: When a plastic ruler is rubbed with a cloth, it becomes charged because:

options.text: Protons move from the cloth to the ruler
Electrons are transferred between the ruler and the cloth

mcq.explanation: Electrons (mobile) move from one surface to the other; protons stay fixed. Exam Tip: Only electrons move in charging by friction.

mcq.questionText: An object that gains extra electrons becomes:
mcq.explanation: Extra electrons give the object an overall negative charge. Exam Tip: Extra electrons = negative charge.

mcq.questionText: An object that loses electrons becomes:
mcq.explanation: Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the object becomes positively charged. Exam Tip: Losing electrons = positive charge.

mcq.questionText: Two objects with the SAME type of charge will:

options.text: Have no effect on each other

mcq.explanation: Like charges push apart, so they repel. Exam Tip: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

mcq.questionText: Two objects with UNLIKE charges will:
mcq.explanation: Opposite charges pull together, so they attract. Exam Tip: Unlike charges attract (+ and -).

mcq.questionText: A material through which electric charge can move easily is called a:
mcq.explanation: Easy movement of charge describes a conductor. Exam Tip: Conductors include metals like copper and aluminium.

mcq.questionText: A material through which electric charge CANNOT move easily is called an:
mcq.explanation: Charge does not move through it easily, making it an insulator. Exam Tip: Insulators include rubber, plastic, glass, and dry wood.

mcq.questionText: A device used to store electric charge is called a:
mcq.explanation: A capacitor stores charge. Exam Tip: Capacitors are used in electronic circuits and camera flashes.

mcq.questionText: A lightning conductor, fixed to the top of tall buildings, works by:

options.text: Attracting lightning and blocking it entirely
Providing an easy path for lightning current to travel safely to the ground
Repelling lightning away from the building

mcq.explanation: A metal conductor and cable give a safe path straight into the earth. Exam Tip: The lightning conductor channels charge to earth, protecting the building.

mcq.questionText: Charging by rubbing two different materials together is called charging by:
mcq.explanation: Rubbing is charging by friction. Exam Tip: Rubbing a plastic ruler or balloon on hair/cloth is charging by friction.

mcq.questionText: Small pieces of paper are attracted to a charged plastic comb because of:

options.text: The electrostatic force of attraction between the charged comb and the paper

mcq.explanation: The charged comb attracts light, uncharged paper by electrostatic force. Exam Tip: This demonstrates static electricity, not magnetism.

mcq.questionText: The charge distribution when a charged object touches a larger conductor, spreading the charge out, results in:

options.text: The charge spreading out and becoming less concentrated

mcq.explanation: Total charge stays the same but spreads over a larger area, becoming less concentrated. Exam Tip: Charge is conserved - it merely redistributes.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is an everyday example of static electricity?

options.text: A small shock felt after touching a metal door handle after walking on a carpet

mcq.explanation: Walking on carpet builds charge by friction; touching metal discharges it, giving a shock. Exam Tip: The bulb example is current electricity; the door-handle shock is static.

mcq.questionText: A charged rod is brought near an uncharged conductor without touching it, and the conductor becomes charged. This process is called:
mcq.explanation: Charging without contact is charging by induction. Exam Tip: Induction = no contact; conduction = direct touching; friction = rubbing.

fib.questionText: An electric charge that remains at rest on an object (not flowing) is called ____ electricity.
fib.explanation: Static electricity is charge that builds up and stays at rest on an object, unlike current electricity which flows. Exam Tip: Static = still; current = flowing.

fib.questionText: When two different materials are rubbed together, the particles that transfer between them are ____.
fib.explanation: Only electrons are mobile and transfer between materials during friction; protons remain fixed in the nucleus. Exam Tip: Only electrons move; protons remain fixed.

fib.questionText: An object that gains electrons becomes ____ charged.
fib.explanation: Gaining extra electrons gives an object more negative charge than positive charge. Exam Tip: More electrons = more negative charge.

fib.questionText: Two objects with like charges ____ each other.
fib.explanation: Like charges push apart because similar charges exert a repulsive force on each other. Exam Tip: Like repel; unlike attract.

fib.questionText: A material that allows electric charge to flow through it easily is called a ____.
fib.explanation: A conductor allows charge to move through it easily. Exam Tip: Metals are good conductors.

fib.questionText: A material that does not allow electric charge to flow through it easily is called an ____.
fib.explanation: An insulator resists the movement of electric charge through it. Exam Tip: Rubber and plastic are common insulators.

fib.questionText: A device used to store electric charge is called a ____.
fib.explanation: A capacitor is designed specifically to store electric charge. Exam Tip: Capacitors store charge for use in electronic circuits.

fib.questionText: A metal rod fixed to the top of a tall building to safely direct lightning to the ground is called a ____.
fib.explanation: A lightning conductor provides a safe, low-resistance path for lightning current to reach the earth. Exam Tip: It gives lightning a safe path to earth.

fib.questionText: Charging an object by rubbing it against another material is called charging by ____.
fib.explanation: Rubbing two materials together transfers electrons, which is charging by friction. Exam Tip: Rubbing a balloon on hair is a classic example.

fib.questionText: Charging a conductor without direct contact, by bringing a charged object nearby, is called charging by ____.
fib.explanation: Induction charges an object without any direct touching, using the electric field of a nearby charged object. Exam Tip: Induction needs no touching.

tf.questionText: Static electricity is charge that stays at rest on an object rather than flowing continuously.
tf.explanation: This is the definition of static electricity, in contrast with current electricity, which flows continuously. Exam Tip: Contrast with current electricity, which flows continuously.

tf.questionText: When materials are rubbed together, protons move from one material to the other.
tf.explanation: Only electrons move during charging by friction; protons stay fixed in the nucleus. Exam Tip: Only electrons move in charging by friction.

tf.questionText: An object that loses electrons becomes positively charged.
tf.explanation: Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, giving a net positive charge. Exam Tip: Losing electrons -> positive charge.

tf.questionText: Like electric charges attract each other.
tf.explanation: Like charges repel each other; only unlike charges attract. Exam Tip: Like repel; unlike attract.

tf.questionText: Metals are generally good conductors of electric charge.
tf.explanation: Metals have free electrons that allow charge to flow easily through them. Exam Tip: Copper and aluminium are excellent conductors.

tf.questionText: Rubber and plastic are good conductors of electricity.
tf.explanation: Rubber and plastic do not allow charge to flow easily, so they are insulators, not conductors. Exam Tip: Rubber/plastic are insulators.

tf.questionText: A capacitor is a device used to store electric charge.
tf.explanation: Capacitors are specifically designed to store electric charge. Exam Tip: Found in electronic devices and camera flash circuits.

tf.questionText: A lightning conductor prevents lightning from striking a building at all.
tf.explanation: A lightning conductor does not stop the strike; it channels the current safely to earth. Exam Tip: It channels the current safely; it does not prevent the strike.

tf.questionText: Charging by induction requires the charged object to touch the conductor being charged.
tf.explanation: Induction charges a conductor without any contact; touching describes conduction instead. Exam Tip: Induction = no touching; conduction = direct contact.

tf.questionText: A small electric shock after touching a metal object, after walking on a carpet, is an example of static electricity discharging.
tf.explanation: Walking on a carpet builds up static charge by friction, and touching metal lets it discharge suddenly as a shock. Exam Tip: A classic everyday demonstration of static charge build-up and discharge.

summary.correctAnswer: An electric charge that builds up and stays at rest on an object, rather than flowing continuously as current.
summary.explanation: It arises from an imbalance of electrons and protons on an object's surface. Exam Tip: Static (at rest) contrasts with current electricity (flowing).

summary.correctAnswer: Charging that occurs when two different materials are rubbed together, causing electrons to transfer from one surface to the other.
summary.explanation: Only electrons move during friction; protons remain fixed in the atoms. Exam Tip: Rubbing a plastic ruler or balloon on cloth or hair is a classic example.

summary.correctAnswer: An object becomes positively charged when it loses electrons, and negatively charged when it gains electrons.
summary.explanation: The overall charge depends on the balance between protons (positive) and electrons (negative). Exam Tip: Lose electrons = positive; gain electrons = negative.

summary.correctAnswer: Like charges repel each other, while unlike charges attract each other.
summary.explanation: This fundamental rule explains why charged objects push apart or pull together. Exam Tip: Like repel; unlike attract.

summary.correctAnswer: A material, such as a metal, through which electric charge can move easily.
summary.explanation: Conductors have free electrons that allow charge to flow through them. Exam Tip: Copper and aluminium are common conductors.

summary.correctAnswer: A material, such as rubber, plastic or glass, through which electric charge cannot move easily.
summary.explanation: Insulators hold their electrons tightly, preventing charge from flowing through. Exam Tip: Insulators are used to cover wires and handles for safety.

summary.correctAnswer: A device used to store electric charge.
summary.explanation: Capacitors are found in electronic circuits and devices such as camera flashes. Exam Tip: Think of a capacitor as a small, temporary charge store.

summary.correctAnswer: A metal spike and cable fixed to the top of a tall building, connected to the earth, to give lightning a safe path to the ground.
summary.explanation: It protects buildings by channelling the lightning current safely to earth instead of through the structure. Exam Tip: It channels charge to earth; it does not stop lightning striking.

summary.correctAnswer: Charging a conductor by bringing a charged object near it, without any direct contact.
summary.explanation: The nearby charge causes electrons in the conductor to redistribute, charging it without touching. Exam Tip: Induction = no contact; conduction = direct touching.

summary.correctAnswer: Common examples include a small shock after touching a metal door handle after walking on a carpet, and small pieces of paper sticking to a charged comb or ruler.
summary.explanation: These effects occur because friction builds up charge, which then discharges or attracts light objects. Exam Tip: Remember that static effects are electrostatic, not magnetic.

hoq.questionText: A student rubs a plastic ruler with wool. The ruler attracts small pieces of paper. Explain using electron transfer.

options.text: Protons move from the cloth to the ruler, making it negative, and this attracts the paper by magnetism
Electrons transfer from the cloth to the ruler, giving the ruler a negative charge, which then attracts the light, uncharged paper by electrostatic force
The ruler gains mass and therefore attracts paper by gravity
Nothing is transferred; the paper moves due to wind

hoq.explanation: Electrons move from cloth to ruler, giving it a negative charge. This attracts uncharged paper electrostatically. Exam Tip: Only electrons move in friction charging; attraction is electrostatic, not magnetism or gravity.

hoq.questionText: A building has a lightning conductor: metal spike, copper cable, earthed plate. Lightning strikes the spike. Explain what happens and why the building is protected.

options.text: The charge disappears completely at the spike
The charge travels safely down the low-resistance copper cable into the earth, instead of passing destructively through the building's structure
The charge bounces back into the clouds
The spike attracts the lightning but does nothing else

hoq.explanation: The copper cable offers a low-resistance path from the spike to the earthed plate, so the current flows safely down rather than through the building. Exam Tip: The key idea is providing an easier, safer path for the charge - the same principle as earthing.

hoq.questionText: Two identical spheres X (+4 units) and Y (-2 units) touch and separate. Determine the charge on each afterwards and whether they attract or repel.
hoq.explanation: Total charge = (+4)+(-2) = +2, shared equally between identical spheres: +1 each. Both have the same charge, so they repel. Exam Tip: For identical conductors in contact, add charges (with sign) then divide by two to share equally.
